newsitem.title: USA: FCC sets task force to probe phone competition.
newsitem.headline: FCC sets task force to probe phone competition.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission Tuesday created a government task force to probe charges that regional Baby Bell companies are unfairly stifling competition in the $100 billion local phone business.

The agency said its "enforcement" task force will identify "trouble spots" and mete out penalties, if necessary, in an effort to open the local market to new competitors after passage of last year's telecommunications law.

The announcement comes after long-distance giants AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. complained that the Bells were thwarting their efforts to offer consumers another source for local service. The Bells deny the charges.
The 1996 Telecommunications Act was designed to allow long-distance providers and other telecom carriers to enter the local phone market controlled by the Baby Bells and GTE Corp.
Aside from building their own facilities, the new entrants are seeking to lease the Bells' huge phone networks in their efforts to win over local customers in the speediest manner.

"There's an immediate need for swift and certain enforcement actions to ensure delivery of the benefits of competition of the 1996 act to the public," FCC Chairman Reed Hundt said. "Enforcement will be fast, fair and predictable."

No. 2 long-distance company MCI applauded Hundt's move as the carrier stepped up its calls for regulators to impose strict deadlines and financial penalties in an effort to pry open local phone monopolies nationwide.

MCI President Timothy Price also said his company's merger plans with British Telecommunications Plc are "going straight ahead" despite steep losses the carrier is running up in the local phone market -- losses that MCI blames on the Bells. He declined to say whether the deal might be restructured.
"It's time for the FCC to set results-oriented, date-certain standards for opening local markets to true competition," Price said in a speech to the Economic Strategy Institute think tank.
He reiterated that MCI's losses in the local market could hit $800 million this year and exceed that amount in 1998.
"The local monopolies have put thick curtains of red tape across the road to competition," he added, charging that some carriers are "outright defiant of the law."

Price said, for example, that some local companies were charging customers nearly $200 in installation fees when switching to MCI local service. Long-distance companies, by contrast, levy a one-time $5 fee, he said.

Price also said the Bells were arguing with customers who request to change over to MCI. And he charged that BellSouth Corp. is sending "retention letters" to MCI customers to keep them from leaving before they are actually switched.
The Bell companies dismissed the allegations.
"We're willing to respond to any real problem that our customers have. But most of these 'problems' are baloney," said BellSouth spokesman John Schneidawind.
"Whatever the FCC looks into, we hope they look at the foot-dragging by the long-distance companies to get into the local phone business," he added. "They have an incentive to stay out our business."

Under the telecom law, the Bells can seek approval to enter the $80 billion long-distance business once their own markets are fully open to competitors. They have been barred from that market since the 1984 breakup of the old AT&T phone monopoly.
